Abstract
The liquid‐phase‐assisted grain growth (LGG) process is a promising strategy
to fabricate large‐grain pure sulfide Cu2ZnSnS4 (CZTS) layers that span the
absorber thickness and improve the carrier collection efficiency in photovol-
taic devices. Li doping is an effective route to promote such LGG process of
Cu2ZnSn(S,Se)4 (CZTSSe) as it can provide liquid Li‐Se phase facilitating the
growth of large‐grain CZTSSe. However, the detailed function of the added Li
in grain growth has rarely been investigated in both CZTS and CZTSSe, as the
reported in situ, and pre‐deposition doping strategies usually suffer from
substantial Li losses during the spin‐coating process and/or the high‐
temperature sulfurization process. Herein, by monitoring the temperature‐
dependent Li loss during the sulfurization process, we demonstrate that a
small proportion of the added Li can remain at the CZTS film from the early
sulfurization stage and provide Li‐S flux to promote the LGG process. An
encouraging efficiency of 10.53%, with a remarkably high short‐circuit current
density of 22.6 mA/cm2 and open‐circuit voltage of 0.744 V, is achieved by a
significantly enlarged grain size of 3 μm with Li addition. This work could
enhance the knowledge of employing Li‐S as flux for growing large‐grain
chalcogenide absorbers for high performance devices with better carrier
transport.

Our recent electron beam induced current (EBIC) and
cathodoluminescence measurements have revealed that
the universal small grain size of CZTS in absorber layer
tends to trigger the loss of short‐circuit current density
(JSC) and fill factor (FF), limiting the device perfor-
mance.10 In this sense, investigating strategies to enlarge
the grain size and reduce recombination in detrimental
grain boundaries in CZTS is one of the promising routes
to further stretch the efficiency of CZTS solar cells.

where the liquid phase is introduced for providing a
capillary force to merge small grains through Ostwald
ripening, is an important process for enlarging the grain
size of CZTS.11 This process has been applied for growing

ses.12–15 However, it is relatively difficult to apply the LGG
process in pure sulfide CZTS, as the melting point of CZTS‐
related metal sulfides (CuxS, ZnS, Cu2SnS3, and SnSx) is
usually beyond the grain growth temperature region of
CZTS.16 Recently, our group reported a low‐temperature
LGG process for CZTS using Na‐rich Cu‐Sn‐S liquid
phase generated from controlled decomposition of a bot-
tom CZTGS nanoparticle layer.17 Although this method
can significantly enhance the overall carrier collection
efficiency in the absorber layer, there is still space for
further improving the JSC as there are still considerable
residual small grains lying between the large grains.

of CZTS is one of the effective approaches to further
promote the LGG process and enlarge the grain size of

Meanwhile, Li doping via post‐deposition treatment

doping strategies reported so far usually trigger massive

state evolution of Li in the absorber during the grain
growth process. The loss of Li was mainly classified as Li‐

our recently reported LGG‐processed CZTS. This method

Cu2Zn(Sn,Ge)S4 (CZTGS) bottom nanoparticle layer.

phase beneath the CZTS layer in our previous CZTGS
modification strategy. Instead, this LiCl addition can
indirectly introduce the additional Li‐S liquid phase via
the controlled decomposition of the Li‐doped CZTGS
bottom layer, promoting the LGG process and the
merging of small CZTS grains. As a result, CZTS films
with a larger grain size of around 3 μm were achieved
with an improved JSC by 2.6 mA/cm2 and 1.4 mA/cm2
compared to the reference and regular CZTGS‐processed
CZTS

respectively.

the evolution of Li species for the Li‐doped CZTS
absorber and obtains an extraordinarily large CZTS grain
size for efficient carrier transport, which can stimulate
the development of kesterite solar cells and other
emerging chalcogenide solar cells.

Record device performance with Li
addition
After depositing an ARC on the best Li‐CZTGS device, we
further achieved a new record efficiency at 10.53% for a
Cd‐free CZTS device (total area), approaching the current
record device performance of CZTS. As shown in
Figure 5A, the Li addition enabled a significantly high JSC

obtained when compared to other reported Cd‐free CZTS

performing device, with the integrated current density

illumination at 1000 W/m2. This value is slightly higher
than the JSC obtained from the total‐area J–V measure-
ment because the EQE measurement has avoided the op-
tical loss from the metal grid shading on devices. Although
the highest EQE has reached 95% at a wavelength of
500 nm, the values between 600 and 750 nm are still lower
than 90%. This indicates that the carrier collection near the
front interface is approaching the limit, while the collec-
tion of carriers in bulk CZTS and near the rear interface
still needs to be improved. Further optimizing the carrier
collection near the rear interface is necessary for JSC boost
and efficiency breakthroughs of CZTS.

CONCLUSION
We have proposed an Li‐enhanced LGG process to
significantly enlarge the grain size of pure sulfide CZTS
by adding LiCl into a CZTGS nanoparticle bottom layer
based on our reported LGG process. The introduction of
LiCl in the CZTGS layer extended the grain size to over
3 μm, resulting in a JSC boost of 1.4 mA/cm2 by reducing
the recombination of minority carriers. A champion Cd‐
free CZTS solar cell was obtained with an efficiency of
10.53% with ARC coating. This work has provided a novel
method to introduce Li into pure sulfide CZTS for fabri-
cating large‐grain CZTS and reducing bulk recombina-
tion and an indication upon the function of Li during the
sulfurization process. Insights into the Li‐enhanced LGG
process can provide indications on the manufacture and
performance optimization of high performance chalco-
genide thin film solar cells.

collection near the rear interface is necessary forJSC boost
and efficiency breakthroughs of CZTS.
3 | CONCLUSION
We have proposed an Li‐enhanced LGG process to
significantly enlarge the grain size of pure sulfide CZTS
by adding LiCl into a CZTGS nanoparticle bottom layer
based on our reported LGG process. The introduction of
LiCl in the CZTGS layer extended the grain size to over
3 μm, resulting in aJSC boost of 1.4 mA/cm2 by reducing
the recombination of minority carriers. A champion Cd‐
free CZTS solar cell was obtained with an efficiency of
10.53% with ARC coating. This work has provided a novel
method to introduce Li into pure sulfide CZTS for fabri-
cating large‐grain CZTS and reducing bulk recombina-
tion and an indication upon the function of Li during the
sulfurization process. Insights into the Li‐enhanced LGG
process can provide indications on the manufacture and
performance optimization of high performance chalco-
genide thin film solar cells.
